content: Pre-eclampsia is a complex disorder of pregnancy that affects multiple organ systems and is characterized by elevated blood pressure and the presence of protein in the urine. This condition is closely linked to endothelial dysfunction. Nitric oxide plays a critical role in the proper functioning of the endothelium, including promoting vasodilation and inhibiting platelet aggregation. It has been suggested that pre-eclampsia may be associated with a deficiency in nitric oxide, although the evidence supporting this hypothesis is inconsistent. Despite this, it has been proposed that agents capable of increasing nitric oxide levels might help prevent the onset of pre-eclampsia. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of nitric oxide donors and precursors in preventing pre-eclampsia and its associated complications. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, and EMBASE, with updates to the search performed as recently as January 2010. The review included randomized trials that specifically assessed the use of nitric oxide donors or precursors for this purpose. Six trials involving a total of 310 women were included in the analysis. Of these, four trials were deemed to be of good quality, while the remaining two were of uncertain quality. Four trials, involving 170 women, compared the use of nitric oxide donors (such as glyceryl trinitrate) or precursors (such as L-arginine) with either a placebo or no intervention. The data from these trials were insufficient to draw reliable conclusions regarding the effects of these agents on the prevention of pre-eclampsia (relative risk [RR] 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49 to 1.41) or its complications. One trial, involving 36 women, compared a nitric oxide donor with nifedipine, while another trial, involving 76 women, compared a nitric oxide donor with antiplatelet agents. Both of these trials were too small to provide reliable conclusions about potential differences in effects between these treatments. The use of glyceryl trinitrate was associated with an increased risk of headache (two trials, 56 women; RR 6.85, 95% CI 1.42 to 33.04) and an increased likelihood of discontinuing treatment (two trials, 56 women; RR 4.02, 95% CI 1.15 to 14.09) when compared to placebo. However, these findings were heavily influenced by extreme results from a single small trial, in which all participants in the treatment group experienced these outcomes (7/7 versus 0/9). In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether nitric oxide donors and precursors are effective in preventing pre-eclampsia or its complications. It is important to note that 13 additional studies, which are awaiting classification, may influence the conclusions of this review once they are assessed.
